learn.title: A point by distance and angle
learn.body: Instead of $(x,y)$, polar coordinates give $(r,\theta)$: go out a distance $r$ from the origin at angle $\theta$. The point $(2,\frac{\pi}{3})$ is 2 units away at $60^\circ$.

learn.title: Converting
learn.body: From polar to rectangular: $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$. From rectangular to polar: $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and $\theta$ from $\tan^{-1}\frac{y}{x}$, checking the quadrant.

learn.title: Rectangular $(-3,3)$ to polar
steps: The point is in quadrant II, so $\theta=135^\circ$, not $-45^\circ$

learn.body: A point has many polar names: adding $360^\circ$ to $\theta$ gives the same point.

questions.prompt: What is $r$ for the rectangular point $(0,5)$?
What is the rectangular $x$ of the polar point $(6,150^\circ)$ to one decimal place?
What is the rectangular $y$ of polar $(6,150^\circ)$?
What is the polar angle of the point $(-3,3)$?
questions.explanation: The point is in quadrant II, so the angle is $135^\circ$.

questions.prompt: What is the rectangular form of $(2,\frac{\pi}{3})$ (to 3 decimals for $y$)?
To go from $(x,y)$ to $r$ we use $r=$ \_\_.
questions.explanation: It is the distance from the origin.

questions.prompt: Match each polar point to its rectangular point.
Does $(3,\theta)$ and $(3,\theta+360^\circ)$ name the same point?
questions.explanation: A full turn returns to the same place.

questions.prompt: Convert $(x,y)$ to polar. Put the steps in order.
questions.explanation: The quadrant check prevents wrong angles.
